name: Fenix Adeyemi-Sørensen
description: Fenix Adeyemi-Sørensen is the most-followed geneware aesthetic figure in M88, known for a long-term modification project they call 'The Slow Bird' — a decade-long series of geneware modifications designed to give them functional bioluminescent plumage, with the explicit acknowledgment that true flight will never be possible and that the beauty of the attempt is the point. Their feathers — grown from engineered follicles along the forearms, shoulders, and spine — shift color with body temperature and emotional state, and are documented in a neural-feed journal that reads more like a meditation practice than a fashion channel. Fenix works exclusively with the independent geneware collective 'Second Flesh' and has been publicly critical of the corporate geneware industry's safety shortcuts.
cultural_impact: Fenix has made geneware modification feel like a long-term philosophical practice rather than a consumer purchase, attracting a following that skews older and more thoughtful than typical aesthetic influencers. Their collaboration with Second Flesh has raised the collective's profile significantly, and their public criticism of corporate geneware safety standards contributed to a 2221 regulatory review that several corponations are still fighting.
key_figures: Dr. Amara Kuznetsova-Ito (Second Flesh lead geneticist)
locations: Second Flesh Collective Lab, Tier 3 Northward District
The Plumage Gallery (pop-up exhibition space Fenix organizes seasonally)
story_hooks: A corporate geneware firm attempts to patent a modification technique that Dr. Kuznetsova-Ito developed at Second Flesh years before the firm claims to have invented it, and Fenix's platform may be the only thing with enough reach to fight the claim publicly.

Fenix's latest modification phase causes an unexpected neurological side effect — their emotional-state color shifts are now broadcasting feelings they can't fully control — and they have to decide whether to document it honestly or go dark.

A young Tier 1 resident reaches out to Fenix with footage of black-market geneware modifications going catastrophically wrong in the Shelf, and asks them to use their platform to expose it — which means stepping into a fight much larger than aesthetics.
platform: The Slow Bird (neural-feed journal, BCI-immersive, independent)
controversy: In 2220, Fenix published side-by-side comparative data showing that three corporate geneware modification chains were using a cheaper follicle-anchoring compound that had a 340% higher long-term rejection rate than the compound Second Flesh uses — data sourced from a corporate internal study that was never published. The corponations claimed the data was stolen. Fenix claimed it was given to them by an employee with a conscience. The regulatory review that followed is ongoing.
